metadata.file_name: 118. Rutkowski et al. (2024). The limits of inference: reassessing causality in international assessments.pdf
metadata.title: The limits of inference: reassessing causality in international assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a conceptual review/critical synthesis of how quasi-experimental causal claims are (and are not) justified when using international large-scale assessment (ILSA) data. It does not analyze an ILSA micro-dataset with a defined analytic sample, nor does it report any application of complex survey weights or replicate-weight variance estimation. As a result, there is no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to specify for estimation. For readers who wish to conduct causal or quasi-experimental analyses with ILSA microdata, the appropriate weights would depend on the specific ILSA Data Explorer/IDB Analyzer workflow and the dataset’s sampling design; however, this paper does not provide those implementation details.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not perform an empirical ILSA-based predictive or causal estimation using student-level cognitive outcomes; instead, it reviews and critiques causal-inference claims and discusses methodological assumptions. Because there is no PV-based achievement modeling step, plausible values handling is not applicable. Missing-data handling is also not reported because no statistical estimation on an ILSA analytic dataset is conducted in this article.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA microdata analytic sample is constructed. The paper synthesizes and critiques prior studies (e.g., quasi-experimental examples using PIRLS/PISA and other designs) rather than estimating models on a new dataset.

data.outcome_summary: This article is not an empirical ML study; it is a methodological critique and framework-oriented review of causal inference attempts using international large-scale assessment (ILSA) data. It argues that the cross-sectional, low-stakes, observational nature of ILSAs and the heterogeneity of educational systems make causal claims tenuous under common quasi-experimental approaches (e.g., potential outcomes framework assumptions, equivalence of groups in expectation, and parallel-trends-like requirements). The paper juxtaposes two higher-quality quasi-experimental exemplars (e.g., voucher lottery and school consolidation) with three ILSA-based quasi-experimental examples (e.g., school closure, private school enrollment, and early tracking), highlighting threats such as non-exogenous treatment exposure, untestable assumptions, and ecological fallacy when treatment/outcomes are measured at higher aggregation levels. It concludes with a cautious evaluation framework and emphasizes that statistical rigor alone cannot guarantee causal validity without strong, context-sensitive assumptions.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is sparse for empirical-data fields because the manuscript is a conceptual review/critical reassessment rather than an original analysis of ILSA microdata. Consequently, there is no defined student analytic sample, no country-level sample-size table, no PV or missing-data handling procedure, and no ML model training/evaluation to extract. The paper’s contribution is methodological: it evaluates the plausibility of causal assumptions in quasi-experimental designs when applied to ILSA contexts.
